regions.name: Middle East
overview: The US–Iran confrontation turned kinetic again around the US midterms. On 2–3 November US forces struck an Iranian anti-aircraft site on Qeshm Island, which Washington called 'defensive' after Iranian fire at a US aircraft and Trump called a 'minor attack'. Over 1–3 November unidentified projectiles hit at least five vessels around Hormuz and the Gulf: a UAE-owned tug sank off Musandam and an Indian dhow crewman was killed. On 4 November the IRGC claimed four tankers were burning after hitting mines and that two vessels had been detained; none of this has been verified. Diplomacy is moving in parallel: Vance has written to Tehran and says he is optimistic, and Qatar is passing proposals in real time. Iran calls the US reply to its seven Hormuz conditions 'unconvincing', and US media report that CENTCOM has strike packages ready.

The Yemen–Saudi war continues at full intensity. The coalition struck Houthi missile and drone assets on 1 November and hit Ras Isa and Bajil in Hodeidah on 2 November, wounding seven according to Houthi media. Saudi air defences intercepted missiles and drones aimed at the south, and civil defence issued alerts for Abha, Khamis Mushait, Taif and Najran. On 4 November the Houthis claimed a new ballistic missile hit on Riyadh's King Khalid airport, which Riyadh has not confirmed. Government forces claimed about 500 Houthis killed in 24 hours on the al-Jawf, Marib and al-Bayda fronts (unverified). The UN reports 290,000 newly displaced. The ICRC reached besieged Taiz on 4 November, its first delivery in more than a month.

Israel's 27 October election produced a certified deadlock. The final results, published on 4 November, give Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats, Eisenkot's bloc 48 and the Arab parties a record 19. Herzog began consultations on 4 November. Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister during what are likely to be long talks, and a repeat election early in 2027 is possible. On the ground, deadly Israeli fire continued in Gaza, with at least 12 killed on 1–2 November, including five police officers. Israel closed the Rafah crossing to aid and travellers on 3 November and ended its 11-day Hebron operation on 2 November, which had displaced more than 4,300 people. A strike in Qabrikha on 4 November caused Lebanon's first reported deaths from Israeli fire since September.

Elsewhere the week was quieter but structurally unchanged. Jordan charged three suspects with terrorism over the Karak church massacre (3 November). Israeli incursions into western Daraa and Quneitra continued, and Syrian forces arrested ISIS members in Deir ez-Zor. ISIS remains active around Hawija in Iraq, where a civilian was kidnapped on 29 October. The UN Security Council renewed UNSMIL in Libya until October 2027, with Russia and Greece abstaining, while Saddam Haftar signed a security protocol with Niger. No significant new incidents were found for Egypt or Tunisia. For Egypt, the main exposure is its authorised but still unannounced military support to Saudi Arabia, which the Houthis call a declaration of war.

countries.name: Gaza
incidents: 1 Nov — al-Mawasi / Khan Younis / Gaza City: Israeli strikes killed at least eight people, according to civil defence, including five Palestinian police officers at a police post in al-Mawasi; a sixth officer later died of his wounds.

2 Nov — southern Khan Younis / al-Musaddar / Tal al-Hawa (Gaza City): A gun attack and an air raid killed two people in Khan Younis, a drone strike killed one in al-Musaddar, and a strike on a vehicle in Tal al-Hawa killed one and wounded five; a community-kitchen minibus was hit in Zeitoun, wounding three. The IDF said it struck fighters in three strikes.

3 Nov — Rafah crossing: Israel turned back travellers and halted aid and commercial trucks from Egypt (about 40 trucks a day), citing smuggling and interference by Hamas security forces; Kerem Shalom was not affected. The Ministry of Health says at least 1,593 people have been killed since the October 2025 ceasefire.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Lethal Israeli fire continues almost daily under the nominal ceasefire, including strikes on Hamas-run police, and the ceasefire death toll has passed 1,590. The closure of the Rafah crossing on 3 November cuts one of the main aid routes as winter sets in, with nearly two million people in need of shelter assistance. Phase two of the ceasefire remains frozen. Israel faces a long coalition process, with Herzog's nominee getting 28 days plus a possible 14-day extension, so no government will be able to take decisions on Gaza until at least December. Over the next 90 days, expect continued drone and air strikes on police and suspected fighters, further creeping advances beyond the Yellow Line, recurring closures of crossings used as leverage, and a severe winter humanitarian crisis. Renewed US/Israel–Iran hostilities would further reduce aid access and international attention.

countries.name: Lebanon
incidents: 4 Nov — Qabrikha (south Lebanon): An Israeli strike on a motorcycle killed one person and wounded another, according to the Health Ministry; Naharnet called these the first such casualties since September.

3–4 Nov — South Lebanon (Baraashit, al-Mansouri, Wadi Zebqine, al-Qantara, Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh, Harees, Hadatha): Overnight Israeli artillery shelling hit several villages; Israeli forces continued demolishing occupied villages, burned homes in Hadatha, and threw stun grenades at farmers in Halta near Kfarshouba.
4 Nov — Beirut: PM Nawaf Salam met President Aoun and warned against dragging Lebanon into 'new futile adventures' amid fears of renewed US–Israeli strikes on Iran.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Israel still occupies a large part of the south and keeps up daily shelling, demolitions and arson. The Qabrikha strike on 4 November ended a weeks-long gap in reported deaths, which confirms that the pattern of lethal fire has not stopped. The main risk over the next 90 days is that Hezbollah is drawn into a renewed US/Israel–Iran war, which now looks more likely after the US strikes on Qeshm and the reported CENTCOM strike packages. That would very probably bring an Israeli air campaign against the Dahiyeh and the Bekaa. Otherwise, expect continued targeted drone strikes, artillery fire and village demolitions in the south, state–Hezbollah friction over disarmament, and a growing security gap as UNIFIL's mandate ends on 31 December. A new Israeli government, whether led by Netanyahu or Eisenkot, is unlikely to change course quickly.

countries.name: Iran
incidents: 2–3 Nov — Qeshm Island: US forces struck an Iranian anti-aircraft facility, which US officials called a 'defensive' response to Iranian surface-to-air fire on US assets; Trump called it a 'minor attack' that 'wasn't war'. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran would respond forcefully.

1–3 Nov — Strait of Hormuz / Gulf of Oman: UKMTO and maritime reporting recorded unidentified projectiles hitting several vessels. The UAE-owned tug Selat Storm sank north-west of Musandam (1 Nov), one Indian crewman was killed on the dhow Al Jusufi off Oman (2 Nov), and the tanker Grit was hit in the engine room off Limah (3 Nov).

4 Nov — South of Hormuz: The IRGC claimed four oil tankers were destroyed and burning after hitting naval mines in a 'prohibited lane', said two other vessels were detained, and claimed it shot down a US MQ-series drone over Qeshm; UKMTO reported no casualties, and CENTCOM has repeatedly disputed Iran's mine claims.

3–4 Nov — Tehran / Doha: SNSC secretary Mohsen Rezaei called the US reply to Iran's seven conditions for reopening Hormuz 'unconvincing', after Vance had written to him proposing direct talks; Qatari mediators visited Tehran and are relaying proposals in real time.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The pause in the war has broken down into direct, if limited, US–Iran exchanges of fire, including US strikes on Qeshm, Iranian fire at US aircraft and drone shoot-down claims. Iran's campaign against shipping at Hormuz goes on, with ships sunk and seafarers killed. Over the next 90 days, there are two plausible paths. In the first, Qatari mediation and the Vance channel produce a framework to reopen Hormuz on terms of 'Hormuz first, nuclear later'; Vance's public linking of the midterm losses to the war strengthens this path. In the second, CENTCOM's prepared strike packages lead to a renewed air campaign, possibly including the underground site at Pickaxe Mountain, which would bring Iranian missile fire at Israel, at US bases in the Gulf and Jordan, and possibly at undersea cables. Expect continued mine and projectile attacks, ship detentions and drone shoot-downs in either case, and continued repression at home.

countries.name: Yemen
incidents: 1 Nov — al-Jawf / Marib / al-Bayda: Government army spokesman al-Nazili claimed 1,272 operations in 24 hours, about 500 Houthi fighters killed and about 170 vehicles or weapons destroyed (not independently verified).

1 Nov — Houthi-held Yemen / Bajil (Hodeidah): The Saudi-led coalition said it struck Houthi ballistic missile and drone resources; two raids on an oil facility in Bajil wounded at least three civilians.
2 Nov — Hodeidah (Ras Isa port, Bajil): Houthi-affiliated media said coalition strikes wounded seven people, four at the Ras Isa dock and three at an oil company site; the coalition did not comment.

4 Nov — Taiz: The ICRC delivered medical supplies to the besieged city for the first time since 23 Sep; the Houthis claimed they downed a Saudi-operated drone over Taiz. The UN says the new fighting has displaced 290,000 people.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Full-scale war continues on several fronts, including al-Jawf, Marib, al-Bayda and Taiz. The coalition is striking Houthi missile infrastructure and Hodeidah's oil and port sites, while the Houthis besiege Taiz and keep firing at Saudi Arabia. The ICRC delivery to Taiz is a small humanitarian opening, but 120 health centres there have stopped working and displacement is rising sharply. Over the next 90 days, expect grinding ground battles without a decisive breakthrough, further coalition strikes on Hodeidah's ports and fuel sites, continued Houthi missile fire at Aden and Saudi Arabia, and a risk of mass civilian deaths in Taiz if supply routes are not reopened. A US–Iran deal could reduce Iranian backing over time, while renewed US strikes on Iran could prompt Houthi threats against US assets and Red Sea shipping.

countries.name: Israel
incidents: 2 Nov — Hebron (West Bank): The IDF ended an 11-day operation launched after the 23 Oct shooting that killed two soldiers; UNICEF, citing the municipality, said 483 families (4,304 people, including 1,845 children) had been displaced as of 30 Oct, and residents reported widespread damage and looting.

2 Nov — West Bank: Israeli police evacuated an illegal outpost, and 18 settlers were detained for assaulting and obstructing security personnel; Palestinian sources reported a wave of settler attacks under military protection overnight into 3 Nov.

4 Nov — Jerusalem: The Central Elections Committee certified the final results (Netanyahu bloc 53, Eisenkot bloc 48, Arab parties 19) and rejected fraud claims; President Herzog began consultations, and the Knesset is to be sworn in on 10 Nov.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. No missile or drone attacks on Israeli territory were found this week, and violence in the West Bank (raids, settler attacks, the aftermath of the Hebron operation) does not amount to hostilities on Israel's own territory. The risk of escalation has risen with the direct US–Iran exchanges and reported US strike preparations. Any renewed US or Israeli campaign against Iran would very likely bring Iranian missile fire and possibly Hezbollah and Houthi attacks, which would move Israel to CRITICAL. Politically, Herzog's nominee will have 28 to 42 days to form a government, and a repeat election in early 2027 is possible. A caretaker Netanyahu government will run security policy in the meantime. Expect continued West Bank raids, settler violence and isolated Palestinian attacks, and sharp polarisation over the role of the Arab parties.

countries.name: Iraq
incidents: 29 Oct — Hawija (Kirkuk province), al-Sayha village: Suspected ISIS militants kidnapped a civilian, prompting a widespread search by security forces.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Little was reported this week, but the underlying threat has not decreased. ISIS cells remain active in the Hawija and Kirkuk belt five weeks after the coalition withdrew, and Iran-aligned factions still resist disarmament, which has been postponed to June 2027. The 27 October drone incident over the Green Zone showed that Baghdad can still be hit now that coalition air defences are gone. Over the next 90 days, the main risk is renewed US–Iran war: the 2–3 November Qeshm strikes make militia drone and rocket attacks on US diplomatic sites and Gulf neighbours, and US or Israeli strikes on PMF positions, a real possibility. Attacks on shipping in the northern Gulf could also hit Basra oil exports. The rapprochement with Damascus is a modest stabilising factor.

countries.name: Saudi Arabia
incidents: 1–2 Nov — Southern region: Saudi air defences destroyed a drone (1 Nov evening) and intercepted a ballistic missile (2 Nov) aimed at the south, according to coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki; Civil Defence issued, then lifted, danger alerts for Abha, Khamis Mushait, Taif and Najran.
2 Nov — Arabian Gulf, about 72 nm east of Ras al-Khafji: A tanker was hit on its port side by two unidentified projectiles; all crew were accounted for and no pollution was reported (UKMTO).

4 Nov — Riyadh / Jizan / Najran: The Houthis claimed a ballistic missile hit on King Khalid International Airport causing 'extensive damage', and claimed attacks on a radar north of Jizan and a military camp in Najran; spokesman Yahya Saree urged airlines to avoid Saudi airspace. Saudi authorities did not comment.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Saudi Arabia remains under recurring Houthi missile and drone attack on its airports, its south and its military sites, and shipping in its Gulf waters is now being hit as well. Riyadh is answering with strikes on Houthi missile infrastructure and the Hodeidah ports, and keeps a security channel open with Tehran. Egypt's authorised support has not yet been visibly deployed. Over the next 90 days, expect continued salvos on Riyadh, Jizan, Najran, Khamis Mushait and the Eastern Province, interception debris and civilian damage, disruption to flights at King Khalid and Dammam, and further departures of events and foreign workers. A renewed US–Iran war would add risk to Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping, while a US–Iran deal could over time weaken Iranian backing for the Houthi campaign.

countries.name: Syria
incidents: 2 Nov — Maariya (Yarmouk Basin, western Daraa): Three Israeli military vehicles entered the village while aircraft flew over the province, according to SOHR; the Sijil Center recorded 395 Israeli-related incidents in October, the highest monthly total this year.
3 Nov — Wadi Abidin (western Daraa) / Quneitra: Israeli vehicles fired toward agricultural land, and Israeli patrols set up checkpoints and detained a civilian in Quneitra.
3 Nov — Deir ez-Zor: Security forces arrested two ISIS members and seized weapons from a hideout linked to a 2025 assassination in al-Mayadin.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Israel continues to hold and patrol a security zone in Quneitra and western Daraa, and incursions were at their highest level of the year in October. Suwayda remains outside state control, and ISIS cells are active from rural Damascus, where two officers were killed on 22 October, to Deir ez-Zor. No deaths were confirmed in this week's reporting, but loss of territorial control and foreign military operations on Syrian soil continue. Over the next 90 days, expect continued Israeli incursions, detentions and occasional killings in the south, possible further Jordanian strikes if Amman ties more attacks to southern Syrian networks, continued ISIS activity in the east and centre, and use of Syrian territory as a corridor if the Iran war resumes. A security deal with Israel is unlikely before a new Israeli government forms.

countries.name: Egypt
incidents: 3 Nov — Rafah crossing (Egypt–Gaza border): Israel halted aid, commercial trucks and travellers entering Gaza from Egypt, including aid from the Egyptian committee; Israel informed the Egyptian coordination bodies in advance. No security incident on Egyptian territory was found in the reporting period.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. No armed violence or terrorist attack on Egyptian territory was found this week. Egypt's exposure is regional rather than domestic: its parliament authorised military support to Saudi Arabia on 26 October, the Houthis have called this a 'declaration of war', and no deployment has been officially announced. The Rafah closure adds pressure on Cairo's mediation role and on the Sinai border zone. Over the next 90 days, the key indicators are the announcement and type of any assets sent to Saudi Arabia (most likely air defence and naval escort), Houthi threats or attacks against Egyptian forces or Suez-bound shipping, and further losses of Suez revenue. HIGH would apply if Egyptian forces come under direct attack, if the Houthis target Suez traffic, or if there is a significant terrorist incident in Sinai.

countries.name: Jordan
incidents: 3 Nov — Amman: The State Security Court prosecutor completed the investigation into the 23 Oct Karak (Hmoud) church attack and charged three suspects, two brothers and a relative by marriage, with terrorism offences, including nine counts of terrorist acts causing death, which can carry the death penalty.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Less than two weeks have passed since the deadliest attack on Jordan's Christians in decades, and Amman retaliated across the border on 26 October with strikes it said killed more than 20 ISIS militants. The threat from armed groups and the risk of further cross-border action remain acute, even though the week itself was quiet. It is not CRITICAL because there is no sustained armed conflict on Jordanian soil. Over the next 90 days, expect a fast-track trial, a continued security crackdown, tighter protection of churches, possible further strikes in southern Syria, and friction with Damascus over coordination. Renewed US–Iran hostilities would very likely bring missile and drone fire at US-used bases in Jordan and debris over its airspace, which would justify CRITICAL. Smuggling of drugs and weapons from Syria remains a constant threat.

countries.name: Libya
incidents: 30 Oct — New York: The UN Security Council adopted resolution 2835, renewing UNSMIL's mandate until 31 Oct 2027 (13 votes in favour; Greece and Russia abstained) after difficult negotiations.

2 Nov — Benghazi: Saddam Haftar and Niger's prime minister signed a strategic cooperation protocol, according to the Libya Observer; no armed clashes or attacks on energy infrastructure were found for the reporting period.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. No armed clashes, drone attacks or blockades were reported this week. UNSMIL's renewal removes the uncertainty about its mandate. The Haftar family's foreign outreach (Niger, Morocco, Türkiye's maritime deal) consolidates the east politically but raises friction with Egypt, Greece and the EU. Over the next 90 days, watch the Haftar succession, disputes over the maritime deal and the central bank, renewed militia fighting in Zawiya and Surman (more than 30 clashes so far in 2026), and drone attacks on the Zawiya refinery and power grid. Any of these on a sustained basis would justify HIGH.

countries.name: Tunisia
incidents: 29 Oct–5 Nov — Tunisia: No new significant security incidents were found in reporting for this period. The most recent events (the 17 Oct anti-Saied rally and the 22–23 Oct police clashes in Ettadhamen and Sfax governorate) fall before the reporting window.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. No new incidents were found this week, but the underlying tension has not eased. The largest anti-Saied protest in years and rare clashes with police over deaths linked to the security forces were followed by further prison sentences for opposition figures and activists, and the state of emergency remains in force until 31 December. There is no organised armed violence, so HIGH does not apply. Over the next 90 days, expect more protests driven by economic hardship and anger at the police, further prosecutions, and a risk of deadly escalation if security forces use more force. HIGH would apply if unrest turns lethal or spreads nationwide. There is also secondary risk from smuggling along the Libyan border.

regions.name: Ukraine/Russia
overview: Diplomacy has started moving but has not slowed the war. The Kremlin says trilateral talks with the US and Ukraine are planned for Abu Dhabi in the first half of November and will focus on post-war security arrangements, but Ushakov again made the start date depend on the 'battlefield situation'. Zelensky hopes for a technical-level meeting between 6 and 10 November and says Washington must set the date. On 31 October Rubio said he was not certain a negotiated deal was possible. The Oleshky local truce held for about six days and let several hundred residents leave, some by plane via Gomel in Belarus. It has now ended, and no wider ceasefire has followed.

Russia's air and glide-bomb campaign was among the deadliest of the year this week. A drone strike on Dnipro railway station killed 15 on 29 October. On 2 November guided bombs, reportedly including a FAB-3000, hit an aid-distribution school and a shelter in Komyshuvakha (Zaporizhzhia), killing at least 40, with about 30 people possibly still under rubble. On 3 November a mass attack with 59 cruise missiles, 17 ballistic missiles and 289 drones hit energy sites in nine regions, and 38 people were killed nationwide that day. On 4 November power and water were cut in Kyiv. Zelensky says interceptor deliveries have fallen threefold compared with 2025, and the newly approved $2.1bn Patriot sale will take years to deliver.

Ukraine has resumed and widened its deep-strike campaign after a mid-October pause. Russian Deputy PM Novak confirmed attacks on three refineries and a gas-chemical complex on 30 October, and two people died at Novokuybyshevsk. The Kstovo (Lukoil-NORSI) refinery near Nizhny Novgorod was set ablaze on 1 November and reportedly struck again on 4 November. A raid on 29–30 October closed all Moscow airports; Sobyanin claimed 862 drones were downed. Ukraine also says it hit Su-34s at Marinovka with Neptune missiles and an Iskander launcher in Kursk Oblast. Kyiv claims October brought record Russian losses (54,400) and a small net territorial gain for Ukraine; neither figure has been verified independently.

The Black Sea remains the most dangerous spillover zone. On 28 October naval drones sank the Liberian-flagged Contship Jet off Bulgaria (crew rescued), at least the ninth merchant vessel hit off Romania and Bulgaria this autumn. On 3 November NATO announced extra maritime patrol aircraft, radars and drones for the area, and Türkiye warned both sides against attacking commercial ships. Elsewhere the periphery stays below the threshold of hostilities. Two Russian drones crossed Moldova on 31 October, forcing airspace closures in the north and centre. Georgia's party-ban case pauses until 9 November, and a UNM politician has been remanded on a treason charge. Armenia's parliament descended into a violent brawl on 29 October. Azerbaijan's border guards shot dead an armed man crossing from Iran on 3 November, and Baku expelled 14 Iranian citizens.

countries.name: Ukraine
incidents: 2 Nov — Komyshuvakha (Zaporizhzhia Oblast): Two waves of Russian guided bombs hit a former school where humanitarian aid was being handed out, then a nearby shelter where people were hiding. Zelensky said the follow-up strike used a FAB-3000. By 4 November the death toll had risen to 40, including rescue workers and police officers, with about 30 more possibly trapped under rubble.

3 Nov — Nationwide/Dnipro/Kharkiv: Russia launched a mass attack with 59 cruise missiles, 17 ballistic missiles (per Zelensky) and 289 drones on energy facilities in nine regions. A morning missile strike on Dnipro killed 2, injured 20 and destroyed a hospice. An overnight bomb hit a Kharkiv hospital passage. Across the country 38 people were killed and more than 150 injured in one day.

29–30 Oct — Dnipro: A Russian drone strike on the railway station killed 15 and injured 14, and Russia struck the station again the next day, injuring a woman and forcing an evacuation. Ballistic missiles fired from Voronezh, Kursk and Bryansk oblasts targeted Kyiv, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.

4 Nov — Kyiv and surrounding regions: An overnight attack with 310 drones (272 downed or suppressed) cut power and water for hours, with energy infrastructure hit in six regions. 6 people were killed and 50 injured nationwide over the past day. The roughly six-day Oleshky ceasefire, which had allowed evacuations, has ended.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Ukraine remains under full-scale attack. Every week brings mass-casualty strikes, such as Komyshuvakha (40+ dead) and Dnipro station (15 dead), and a systematic missile and drone campaign against the energy grid ahead of winter. Over the next 90 days, expect Russia to keep combining cruise, ballistic and jet-drone salvos against power, water and rail hubs, and to rely more on heavy glide bombs (FAB-3000) against front-line towns in Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Kharkiv oblasts. The stated threefold fall in interceptor deliveries and the years-long lead time on the $2.1bn Patriot sale mean outages in Kyiv and the east will get worse. The planned technical-level trilateral in Abu Dhabi (Kyiv hopes for 6–10 November) is the main diplomatic variable. Moscow ties its timing to battlefield conditions, so a general or energy ceasefire within 90 days is unlikely. More localised humanitarian arrangements like Oleshky, prisoner exchanges and evacuation corridors are the most plausible results. Kyiv will keep up deep strikes on refineries and airfields as leverage. Watch whether the Abu Dhabi talks actually convene, whether the Oleshky model is repeated, how much generating capacity is lost after each mass strike, and the pace of Russian pressure on the Pokrovsk and Zaporizhzhia axes.

countries.name: Russia
incidents: 29–30 Oct — Moscow region: A mass Ukrainian drone raid closed all Moscow airports overnight. Sobyanin first spoke of 613 drones and later said 862 were destroyed between the evening of 29 October and the morning of 30 October. These are Russian official figures and could not be independently verified.

30 Oct — Novokuybyshevsk (Samara Oblast) and other sites: A drone attack set the Novokuybyshevsk refinery on fire, and Governor Fedorishchev said two people died while clearing debris. Deputy PM Novak confirmed attacks on three refineries and a gas-chemical complex. Ukraine's Navy said that on 29 October it hit two Su-34s at Marinovka airfield (Volgograd Oblast) with Neptune missiles, and the General Staff said it struck an Iskander-M launcher near Fatezh (Kursk Oblast).

1 Nov — Kstovo (Nizhny Novgorod Oblast): A massive overnight drone attack set the Lukoil-NORSI refinery, one of Russia's largest, on fire. Governor Nikitin said an industrial facility was significantly damaged, with no casualties, and Ukraine's Fire Point claimed the strike. Ukrainian outlets reported a second strike on the site on the night of 4 November.

4 Nov — Adygeysk (Adygea)/nationwide: Russia's Defence Ministry claimed it shot down 709 Ukrainian drones overnight. A drone attack started a fire at an Ozon logistics centre in Adygeysk, with no casualties reported. Earlier, on 31 October, explosions were reported in Ufa amid drone alerts.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Russia is waging an active war, and its own territory is under sustained attack. Mass drone raids now regularly close every Moscow airport, refineries in Samara, Nizhny Novgorod and elsewhere are being hit again after a mid-October pause and are causing deaths, and strikes extend to airbases and missile launchers. Over the next 90 days, expect the Kremlin to use the Abu Dhabi track to seek US concessions, including sanctions relief and the exclusion of Europe, while holding the timing hostage to 'battlefield conditions'. It is unlikely to concede on territory or agree to a general ceasefire, and localised humanitarian gestures such as Oleshky serve as goodwill signals. Expect the winter campaign against Ukraine's energy system to continue, with heavy use of FAB-3000-class glide bombs at the front. Deniable attacks on Black Sea shipping are also likely to continue, which keeps a NATO–Russia incident possible now that NATO is reinforcing maritime surveillance. Ukraine's deep strikes will keep hitting fuel output and aviation and may cause regional fuel shortages. The regime's internal grip remains firm, and stability risk is low.

countries.name: Belarus
incidents: 31 Oct — Gomel: Four evacuation flights carrying hundreds of residents from occupied Oleshky (Kherson Oblast) landed in Gomel, from where evacuees continued to Ukrainian-controlled territory, making Belarus a transit point for the US-brokered humanitarian arrangement.

3 Nov — Minsk: At the 4th Minsk International Conference on Eurasian Security, Lukashenka warned that protests across Europe driven by living costs could spread to and destabilise Belarus, and repeated his offer to host peace talks.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. There are no hostilities on Belarusian territory and no troop build-up on the Ukrainian border was reported this week. The country's profile remains indirect support for Russia's war, through drone relays and logistics, combined with militarisation and coercive signalling toward NATO neighbours. Over the next 90 days, expect Minsk to present itself as a humanitarian and diplomatic facilitator, as with the Oleshky transit and its offer to host talks, to gain leverage in its prisoner-for-sanctions bargaining with Washington. Envoy Coale's next Minsk visit has reportedly been delayed. Expect continued balloon smuggling and border friction with Lithuania and Latvia during the winter season, more territorial-defence readiness drills, and continued domestic repression. A rise to HIGH would require direct military coercion of a NATO neighbour, a serious armed border incident, or Belarusian forces joining the war.

countries.name: Moldova
incidents: 31 Oct — Rîbnița/Telenești/Călărași and Soroca/Edineț districts: During large Russian attacks on Ukraine, two drones violated Moldovan airspace. One flew in from Ukraine's Odesa region over the Transnistrian region (Rîbnița) to Călărași; the second crossed from Vinnytsia Oblast via Dondușeni and Edineț. The Defence Ministry temporarily closed airspace over the north and centre. No crashes or casualties were reported.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Drone violations of Moldovan airspace remain a pattern: two more crossed on 31 October, after a 23 October crash near homes that led Chișinău to expel a Russian diplomat. There are still no casualties, however, and no deliberate strike on Moldova, so the HIGH threshold is not met. Over the next 90 days, expect more incursions, temporary airspace closures and possible debris impacts whenever Russia launches mass attacks on Odesa and Vinnytsia regions, often routed over Transnistria. Expect further diplomatic protests, faster EU-funded air-surveillance and counter-drone purchases, and continued Russian hybrid pressure, including cyber activity, Gagauzia and the winter energy squeeze on Transnistria. Attacks on shipping off Romania also threaten Moldova's trade routes. A first drone fatality, damage to critical infrastructure, or evidence of deliberate targeting would justify reviewing the level toward HIGH.

countries.name: Georgia
incidents: 4 Nov — Tbilisi: UNM politician Giorgi Baramidze was remanded in custody on a treason (sabotage) charge over remarks about the 1992–93 Abkhazia conflict. Opposition leaders briefed diplomats on the party-ban case, and PM Kobakhidze said Georgia aims to 'catch up' with Ukraine and Moldova, which have banned parties.

30 Oct–2 Nov — Tbilisi: Oral submissions in the Constitutional Court case to ban five opposition parties ended on 30 October, and hearings resume on 9 November. ALDE, the Norwegian Helsinki Committee and the OSCE PA criticised the case. Tbilisi's 46th consecutive Saturday march passed without reported violence.

31 Oct — Bershueti / South Ossetia line: A Georgian citizen detained by Russian forces near Bershueti was released through the EU Monitoring Mission hotline. Separately, a Georgian man detained after crossing into South Ossetia was returned.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. There is no organised political violence. Repression takes the form of prosecutions, which now include a treason charge against an opposition politician for his statements, administrative detentions, and the pending party-ban case. Weekly protests remain peaceful, and 'borderisation' detentions along the South Ossetia line continue at a low, routine level. Over the next 90 days, expect hearings to resume on 9 November in a court that has rejected every opposition motion. A ruling could be timed around the Opposition Alliance's 28 November rally, and the legal deadline is June 2027. Expect more criminal cases against opposition figures, election-law changes that narrow appeals, deeper conflict with the EU after the 2026 Enlargement Package, and the Geneva International Discussions on 10–11 November. Banning the main opposition parties, combined with mass protests that are violently dispersed, would justify HIGH.

countries.name: Armenia
incidents: 29 Oct — Yerevan: A brawl broke out in parliament between Civil Contract and Strong Armenia MPs. Deputy Speaker Aleksanyan threw a chair, bottles were thrown, and several MPs left with injuries. Pashinyan called the response 'proportionate and right' and blamed the opposition, while the Human Rights Defender condemned the violence.

3–4 Nov — Yerevan: Pashinyan warned that blocking the planned constitutional referendum would be 'a rejection of lasting peace' with Azerbaijan, and the opposition alleged repression. Armenia is gradually taking over border control from Russian forces, and Pashinyan ordered design work to begin on the TRIPP (Trump Route) rail, road and power lines.

4 Nov — Yerevan: The Investigative Committee said the Azerbaijani soldier detained in Shaki (Syunik) on 1 October crossed the border illegally and that there is no evidence he intended to kill anyone, keeping the incident framed as an individual case.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. There are no hostilities and no fatal border incidents. Tension is political and has become more physical: the 29 October parliamentary brawl injured MPs, and Pashinyan's rhetoric toward the opposition is increasingly hostile. This is still limited violence, not organised political violence. Over the next 90 days, expect the government to publish the draft constitution in November and push toward a referendum, which Baku makes a condition for signing the peace treaty. That will deepen polarisation with Strong Armenia and the church-aligned opposition, and may bring more prosecutions of opposition MPs. Expect TRIPP design work and EU-alignment steps to continue, alongside a gradual reduction of Russia's border role. Moscow will answer with economic and diplomatic pressure rather than force. Armed border incidents, a deliberate shooting, or violent street unrest around the referendum would warrant a review toward HIGH.

countries.name: Azerbaijan
incidents: 3 Nov — Geytepe (Iranian border): Border guards shot dead a man who was trying to cross illegally and who reportedly opened fire on them, and Tehran was notified. Drones were also neutralised on the border, and 136.6 kg of drugs were seized in three smuggling attempts.

4 Nov — Baku: Azerbaijan declared 14 Iranian citizens persona non grata over statements it called hostile. The closed preliminary hearing began against Popular Front chairman Ali Karimli and his deputy, who face charges of attempting to seize power; the trial on the merits starts 13 November.

2 Nov — Baku: APA TV reporter Sanan Bahramli was assaulted while covering a fire at a timber market, and a suspect was detained. The trial of 12 Meydan TV journalists on currency-smuggling charges continues.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. There are no hostilities on Azerbaijani territory. The armed border incident with an Iranian smuggler and the expulsion of 14 Iranians show friction with Tehran, but not military escalation. Domestic pressure takes the form of prosecutions: the Karimli coup case, the Meydan TV and Toplum TV cases, and a school-uniform rule that effectively bans hijabs, which has drawn protest. Lethal political violence has not occurred. Over the next 90 days, expect the 13 November Karimli trial and Victory Day on 8 November to bring heightened security and nationalist messaging. Expect continued in-absentia charges against critics abroad and tensions with Iran, balanced by closer ties with Israel and Georgia. The Armenia track is slow but stable, and progress depends on Yerevan's constitutional referendum. Violent clashes during protests, or a pattern of armed incidents on the Armenian or Iranian border, would warrant a review toward HIGH.

regions.name: Sahel
overview: Sudan's war is getting wider and harder on infrastructure. On 3 November the RSF and SPLM-N (al-Hilu) reportedly took the Sali military base in Blue Nile, about 100 km south of Ed Damazin, days after the army said it had repelled attacks there. On 4 November an overnight RSF drone attack on Ed Damazin killed two people. Between 26 October and 2 November RSF drones repeatedly hit power stations, fuel depots and army sites across army-held Sudan, including Shendi, Al Dabbah, Merowe, Kassala and Rabak, causing widespread outages. On 3–4 November the UN warned that these strikes are disrupting electricity, water and fuel supplies, and that hundreds of aid trucks are stranded for lack of fuel.

Kordofan stays the most violent front. A drone strike at El Dibo reportedly killed eight people on 2 November. On 3 November Brig. Gen. Haroun Mersal, the Joint Darfur Force's operational commander in Kordofan, was killed in combat at Um Shaeira. On 4 November a suspected army Antonov strike on a water source at Um Badr (North Kordofan) killed two women and wounded ten, during a second day of army operations on the North/West Kordofan border. The Khartoum government also accuses Ethiopia of a role in drone attacks on its power infrastructure, adding a cross-border risk in the Blue Nile theatre.

In Nigeria, jihadist and bandit violence continued in several regions. The military reported killing four senior ISWAP commanders after an attack on its positions in Kukawa (Borno) on the night of 31 October, and 34 suspected Boko Haram fighters in Lake Chad operations on 28–30 October. On 3 November bandits ambushed a police convoy guarding a ruling-party Senate primary in Tsafe (Zamfara), killing at least eight security personnel and seizing rifles. This shows how insecurity now overlaps with the pre-election calendar. Killings also continued in Benue and Plateau.

In the central Sahel and Chad, very little was reported. No independently verified attack was found in Mali, Niger or Burkina Faso for 29 Oct–5 Nov. The only output was Malian army strike communiqués (Operation Dougoukoloko) and a 4 November HRW report documenting JNIM massacres at a Burkinabè gold-mine site in September. This reflects junta information blackouts, not calm. The Niger–Chad dispute over the 24 October Emiloulou drone strike is unresolved, with Niamey pressing for UN Security Council and AU referral. No new official information came out of Chad's Tibesti fighting.

countries.name: Mali
incidents: 30 Oct — Bamako: The army general staff reported Operation Dougoukoloko air strikes carried out on 28 Oct near Talhandak, on nine motorbikes at Nangola (Dioïla circle) and about 32 km west of Djenné. It said no movement was seen after the strikes and gave no toll.

29 Oct–5 Nov — Nationwide: No independently verified jihadist or FLA attack on FAMa, the Africa Corps or civilians was found for the week. This is consistent with the junta's restrictions on reporting, not a sign that violence has eased.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. JNIM, the FLA and the Islamic State Sahel hold territory and have carried out mass-casualty attacks in recent weeks: the Dioura base in September and Tagadayat near Ménaka in October. The army's continuing strikes in Ségou, Mopti, Koulikoro and Timbuktu show hostilities are ongoing, so a week without verified reporting does not justify a lower level. Over the next 90 days FAMa and the Africa Corps will likely try to consolidate around Kidal and push toward Aguelhok and Tessalit. In the centre and west they will keep relying on drone and air strikes whose documented civilian toll feeds JNIM recruitment. JNIM remains the main threat to the state, through garrison assaults, IEDs around Mopti/Sévaré and pressure on the fuel corridors from Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire. Escorted tanker convoys are a likely target as the dry season sets in. IS Sahel reprisals against Tuareg and Daoussahak communities near Ménaka are likely to recur. Watch for a large garrison assault, a renewed blockade announcement, or signs of strain inside the junta after the September losses.

countries.name: Niger
incidents: 29 Oct–5 Nov — Niamey/Agadez: The dispute over the 24 Oct Emiloulou drone strike (two civilians killed) continued. Niger says it has physical and technical evidence implicating Chad, with French support, and is seeking referral to the UN Security Council and the AU Peace and Security Council. Chad denies involvement and has asked Niamey to publish its evidence.
29 Oct–5 Nov — Tillabéri/Tahoua/Dosso: No independently verified attack on state forces or civilians was found. Under the junta's reporting restrictions this is an information gap, not a lull.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained: the threat has not decreased. Recent signals point to sustained insurgency and acute regime instability: ISSP mass-casualty attacks on soldiers and gendarmes through July–September, the attempted coup or mutiny, and the continuing army purge. A further week without verified reporting does not indicate calm. Over the next 90 days ISSP ambushes on convoys and posts in Tillabéri and attacks in the Tahoua–Dosso belt are likely to continue. JNIM is likely to keep pressing in the south-west toward Benin, and Boko Haram/ISWAP to keep attacking around Diffa and N'Guigmi. The Emiloulou dispute gives Niamey a nationalist rallying point against alleged French and Chadian interference. Chad's counter-accusation that Niger harbours Chadian rebels raises the risk of proxy activity along the shared northern border. An Algerian deployment at Madama would add a new foreign military actor in the north, but will not affect the south-western insurgency. Another coup or mutiny remains a realistic risk.

countries.name: Burkina Faso
incidents: 4 Nov — Yatenga province: Human Rights Watch reported that JNIM fighters killed 24 civilians and wounded at least 20 in a 1 Sep attack on the Soubo artisanal gold-mining site (Ouahigouya district), and that an IED near Mera killed three civilians on 5 Sep. It cited ACLED's count of 125 JNIM attacks in Burkina Faso between January and August that killed 188 civilians.
29 Oct–5 Nov — Nationwide: No independently verified attack on army or VDP positions was found, in line with the junta's continuing information blackout.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Two jihadist groups fight the state and each other across much of the country, and the HRW findings confirm continued mass killing of civilians. The absence of reported attacks reflects the blackout, not calm. Over the next 90 days the JNIM–IS Sahel contest for Oudalan and Liptako-Gourma, which began at Ganadaouri on 9 Oct, will likely keep producing high-casualty clashes. JNIM will likely keep overrunning army and VDP posts in the North, East and Boucle du Mouhoun and keep up the sieges of Djibo, Sebba and Titao, with large garrison assaults likely as the dry season sets in. Artisanal gold sites remain high-risk targets. The reinstated death penalty points to harsher repression of dissent and suspected collaborators, and the reported reliance on Russian guards for Traoré shows continuing regime-security concerns. Analysts should rely on group claims, displacement data and rights-group reporting, and watch for instability inside the junta.

countries.name: Sudan
incidents: 3 Nov — Sali, Blue Nile: The RSF and SPLM-N (al-Hilu) reportedly captured the strategic Sali military base, about 100 km south of Ed Damazin, a day after the army's 4th Infantry Division said it had repelled attacks on Sali and Bakori. Sudans Post geolocated footage of RSF fighters in the town, but the coalition's claims of heavy army losses are unconfirmed and the army had not commented by publication.

4 Nov — Um Badr, North Kordofan: A suspected army Antonov air strike hit a water source in the Dar Bahr neighbourhood, killing two women, wounding ten and destroying the Al-Kabjark water station. It came on a second day of army operations against the RSF on the North/West Kordofan border.
3 Nov — Um Shaeira, North Kordofan: Brig. Gen. Haroun Mersal, the Joint Darfur Force's operational commander in Kordofan, was reported killed in combat.

4 Nov — Ed Damazin, Blue Nile: An overnight RSF drone attack on military and civilian infrastructure reportedly killed two people. It followed a wave of RSF drone strikes on power stations and fuel depots from 30 Oct to 2 Nov, at Shendi, Al Dabbah (where one woman was killed), Merowe, Aroma and Halfa El Jadida, which caused widespread outages.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained: full-scale war continues on several fronts. The army is losing ground in Blue Nile, both sides are trading deadly air and drone strikes in Kordofan, and the RSF is running a systematic drone campaign against power and fuel infrastructure deep in army-held territory. Over the next 90 days the RSF–SPLM-N alliance is likely to exploit the fall of Sali and push toward Dindiro and Ed Damazin, while the army tries to retake lost bases. Khartoum's accusation that Ethiopia is involved raises the risk of a cross-border dimension. In Kordofan, fighting around El Obeid, Um Shaeira and the North/West Kordofan border is likely to intensify, with continued army Antonov and drone strikes on RSF-held areas and RSF drone attacks on army-held cities. Further mass-casualty strikes on markets and mines, like Nyala and Abyei in October, are likely. The infrastructure campaign will deepen electricity, water and fuel shortages and strand humanitarian convoys, worsening famine conditions. With foreign arms flows continuing and no credible talks, a truce is unlikely. Expect continued displacement into Chad, South Sudan and Ethiopia.

countries.name: Chad
incidents: 29 Oct–5 Nov — N'Djamena/Niamey: The dispute with Niger over the 24 Oct Emiloulou drone strike continued, with Niger seeking UN Security Council and AU referral. Chad maintains it did not conduct or support any strike and backs an independent international inquiry.

29 Oct–5 Nov — Tibesti: No new official information on the fighting with the Miski Self-Defence Committee. The government has still made no statement after AFP reported on 28 Oct that at least 72 soldiers had been wounded since 14 Oct, so the lack of news is not evidence that the clashes have ended.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained, with upward pressure. Chad faces sustained army clashes with a militia that holds Miski in Tibesti, spillover drone strikes from the Sudan war on its eastern border (Bamina, 20 Oct), Boko Haram attacks around Lake Chad, and a deepening dispute with Niger. It is not raised to CRITICAL because the Tibesti fighting is confined to one mining area, confirmed deaths remain limited and the state controls the wider territory. Over the next 90 days the army is likely to try to retake Miski by force, which could produce a confirmed high death toll and draw in Toubou networks and Libyan-based rebels. That, sustained weekly deadly clashes, or repeated large cross-border strikes would justify CRITICAL. The Niger dispute is likely to keep escalating rhetorically, with a risk of mutual support for rebel groups along the northern border. The new military cooperation accords with France will feed Niamey's narrative. Dry-season transhumance will likely bring more farmer–herder violence in Salamat and Ouaddaï. Boko Haram raids on Lake Chad islands remain likely, and refugee arrivals at Tiné and Adré will stay high as fighting in Darfur and Kordofan continues.

countries.name: Mauritania
incidents: 29 Oct–5 Nov — Nationwide: No security incident on Mauritanian territory was reported in open sources this week.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. The country has no organised armed violence at home; its risk comes from border friction with Mali, pressure from more than 300,000 Malian refugees in Hodh Chargui, Atlantic migration flows and limited social unrest, such as the late-October student fare protests. Over the next 90 days FAMa and Africa Corps strikes in the Timbuktu and Ségou regions near the border, together with JNIM activity in western Mali, are likely to push more refugees into Hodh Chargui. They also raise the risk of drone or ground incidents involving Mauritanian herders, keeping relations with Bamako tense. Nouakchott will likely stick to containment through diplomatic protests and precautionary measures, while migrant boat interdictions and expulsions continue. A JNIM attack inside Mauritania or an armed border clash would justify HIGH.

countries.name: Nigeria
incidents: 3 Nov — Near Gidan-Giye, Tsafe LGA, Zamfara: Attackers ambushed a bus carrying security personnel deployed for a ruling-party Senate primary. They killed at least eight (five police officers and three Community Protection Guard members), seized five AK-47s and abducted an unconfirmed number of officers.

31 Oct — Kukawa LGA, Borno: The army (Operation Hadin Kai) said it repelled an ISWAP attack on its positions with air support and killed four senior commanders, including Shura Council member Abu Hajara and Abul Walid, a close associate of ISWAP leader Ba Shuwa. The claim is not independently verified.

30 Oct — Dumba, Lake Chad (Borno): Navy marines and the Army 403 Amphibious Brigade attacked a suspected Boko Haram enclave, part of 28–30 Oct operations in which the navy said at least 34 insurgents were killed, figures it called subject to verification.

4 Nov — Logo LGA, Benue / Barkin Ladi LGA, Plateau: Suspected bandits killed four people and wounded five at Abeda Shitile market in Benue, according to residents. In Plateau, gunmen killed an 18-year-old vigilante in Rachas village and abducted two visually impaired people.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Repeated ISWAP and Boko Haram attacks on army positions in Borno and Yobe, a bandit ambush that killed police guarding an electoral event, and continued killings in Benue and Plateau, after October's 62-death massacre in Taraba, confirm sustained insurgency and large-scale armed violence across several regions. Over the next 90 days ISWAP is likely to keep up night raids on forward bases in Kukawa, Guzamala, Marte and the Lake Chad islands as dry-season mobility improves, along with IED and ambush attacks on supply routes. The military will claim high enemy tolls from air and amphibious operations, but these are hard to verify. Bandit groups in Zamfara, Katsina and the middle belt are likely to target security forces and party events as primaries proceed, which will politicise insecurity ahead of the election cycle. Farmer–herder and reprisal violence in Plateau and Benue is likely to continue.

regions.name: Asia-Pacific
overview: The Korean peninsula had its busiest week of 2026. On 29 October North Korea fired around ten to a dozen short-range ballistic missiles from Wonsan, each flying about 250 km. The same morning, a day after Seoul renewed its offer of military talks on the MDL, test loudspeaker broadcasts were heard in Paju for four to five hours. On 31 October Pyongyang tested a cluster-bomb warhead for tactical ballistic missiles and said it would deploy four warhead types to units by year's end. On 4 November it fired more missiles from Sondok, possibly Hwasong-11 variants. Pyongyang has not answered the talks offer, so the DMZ remains the region's most likely point of a kinetic clash.

Pakistan's two-front war continued at high tempo. On the Afghan border, Pakistani and Taliban forces clashed at Torkham on 1 November over a new Taliban checkpoint, the third Torkham clash in a week. They traded fire again in South Waziristan on 1–2 November, and the Taliban say Pakistani fire killed a civilian in Paktika's Shkin district. Mediation by China, Russia, Turkey and Saudi Arabia has not produced a ceasefire. In Balochistan, the BLA claims more than 25 attacks and over 40 troops killed between 26 October and 3 November, concentrated in Kharan, Nushki, Mastung and Kech. ISPR has not commented and the figures are unverified. In Lakki Marwat (KP) on 4 November police killed two militants, one of them a suicide bomber.

Chinese pressure on the first island chain rose again after a quieter October. In the 24 hours to 06:00 on 3 November, Taiwan's MND tracked 49 PLA aircraft, 6 warships and 6 official ships, a jump that analysts called an unannounced 'quiet exercise'. At Scarborough Shoal, a PCG flight on 29 October counted three CCG ships, five militia vessels and a PLAN warship, plus an unidentified Chinese vessel carrying a sensor-fitted craft inside the lagoon. On 30 October the PLA Southern Theater Command announced naval and air 'combat-readiness patrols' around the shoal. Japan scrambled fighters on 2 November against WZ-7 high-altitude reconnaissance drones passing between Okinawa and Miyako.

Myanmar's air war killed civilians across several regions this week. The Irrawaddy recorded nine regime airstrikes between 29 October and 1 November that killed 16 people and injured 51. On 1 November alone, according to the Arakan Army, strikes on four Rakhine townships killed at least 12 civilians, including a newborn at a Mrauk-U maternity clinic. A school bombing in Loikaw on 31 October killed three children. Elsewhere violence was deadly but local. In Manipur, five Kuki men were killed on 31 October–1 November and a Naga factional gunfight in Noney on 4 November killed three to four militants. In Bangladesh, garment workers clashed with police over wages in Mirpur and Gazipur on 2–3 November.

countries.name: North Korea
incidents: 29 Oct — Wonsan, east coast: The JCS said North Korea fired around ten to a dozen short-range ballistic missiles toward the East Sea at about 12:30 local time, each flying roughly 250 km. The salvo came a day after Unification Minister Chung Dong-young renewed Seoul's 23 Oct offer of military talks on the MDL.

29 Oct — Western DMZ, opposite Paju: North Korea appeared to test its anti-South propaganda loudspeakers. Broadcasts were heard in Paju from 06:00 for four to five hours at low volume, following Kim Yo Jong's end-of-October deadline.

31 Oct — Undisclosed site (KCNA, 1 Nov): The Missile Administration tested a 'Standard Type 2' cluster-bomb warhead for tactical ballistic missiles and claimed it can devastate 12–13 hectares. Pyongyang said four warhead types will be deployed to units by year's end.

4 Nov — Sondok, South Hamgyong: North Korea fired multiple missiles toward the East Sea that flew under 300 km; analysts suspect Hwasong-11 'Ra' tactical ballistic missiles. The launch coincided with the US midterm elections.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. The testing tempo has clearly risen, with three launch or test events between 29 Oct and 4 Nov, including a salvo of about a dozen SRBMs and a cluster-warhead trial tied to an end-of-year deployment pledge. Over the next 90 days, expect further salvo launches of Hwasong-11-family missiles, some timed to allied drills or to US political events. Expect the loudspeaker campaign to move from tests to sustained broadcasts, and DMZ fortification work to keep crossing the MDL. That will draw South Korean warning fire, which Pyongyang frames as grounds for 'self-defence'. Pyongyang is likely to keep ignoring Seoul's MDL talks offer. A mass salvo toward the Northern Limit Line or an exchange of fire at the DMZ is the main escalation path. A nuclear test remains a low-probability wildcard.

countries.name: Myanmar
incidents: 1 Nov — Kyauktaw, Mrauk-U, Kyaukphyu and Pauktaw, Rakhine State: According to the Arakan Army, junta jets and a Y-12 killed at least 12 civilians and wounded 32. A strike on a bridge in Kyauktaw killed seven pedestrians, and cluster bombs dropped near a temporary clinic and maternity ward in Mrauk-U killed five, including a newborn.
31 Oct — Wanngawt village, Loikaw Township, Karenni State: Two regime fighter jets and a Y-12 bombed a school during a holiday meal programme, killing three children and injuring eight.

29 Oct–1 Nov — Nationwide: The Irrawaddy recorded nine regime airstrikes in four days that killed 16 people and injured 51. DMG reported heavy junta–AA clashes in Sittwe, alongside an airstrike on a Buddhist monastery in Kyauktaw.

1–3 Nov — Indaw Township, Sagaing: After taking heavy losses in October, a reinforced junta column resumed its offensive near Kyaungkone village, backed by Mi-35 helicopter fire, a jet strike and night Y-12 bombing, which forced residents of nearby villages to flee.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. The regime's air campaign is causing mass civilian casualties in Rakhine, Karenni and Sagaing, and ground fighting is heavy at Sittwe and Indaw. Over the next 90 days, expect the AA to keep tightening its siege of Sittwe and the junta to answer with more air and naval bombardment of Kyauktaw, Mrauk-U, Pauktaw and the Kyaukphyu approaches. Mass-casualty strikes on clinics, schools and bridges are likely to recur. In the north, troops freed by China-brokered ceasefires are likely to keep pushing up the Mandalay–Sagaing corridor toward Tigyaing, Katha and Indaw ahead of the regime's election plans, with displacement and scorched-earth tactics. Loss of Sittwe would be a strategic turning point and would increase Chinese involvement around Kyaukphyu. No negotiated de-escalation is in sight.

countries.name: Pakistan
incidents: 1 Nov — Torkham crossing, Khyber: Pakistani and Afghan Taliban forces clashed from about midday after the Taliban tried to set up a checkpoint near the crossing, the third Torkham clash in a week. Humanitarian staff withdrew and the Taliban evacuated a camp for deportees.

1–2 Nov — South Waziristan border / Shkin, Paktika: Pakistan said it struck several Afghan Taliban border posts and mortar positions after 'unprovoked' fire on its checkpoints, with no Pakistani casualties. Taliban police said Pakistani fire on Sordagh village in Shkin district killed a young man and wounded two civilians.

26 Oct–3 Nov — Kharan, Nushki, Mastung, Kech and Gwadar, Balochistan: The BLA claims more than 25 attacks killing over 40 personnel, including an IED and a five-hour clash at Lejay, Kharan (1 Nov), the seizure of Muskan Qalat police station (31 Oct) and a convoy attack near Mastung (2 Nov). ISPR has not commented and none of the figures are verified.
4 Nov — Lakki Marwat, KP: Police killed two militants, one of them a suicide bomber, after the occupants of a vehicle opened fire on a police team; a third militant escaped wounded.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Over the next 90 days, near-daily cross-border fire with the Afghan Taliban at Torkham, Kurram and South Waziristan is likely to continue, with a high risk of renewed Pakistani air strikes inside Afghanistan if a mass-casualty TTP attack occurs. Multi-party mediation has not produced a ceasefire. In Balochistan, the BLA's sustained campaign of convoy ambushes, IEDs, police-station seizures and highway 'economic blockades' (Quetta–Taftan) will continue, and casualty claims will keep diverging sharply from official accounts. In KP, TTP-linked attacks on police and troops will remain frequent, with suicide and VBIED attacks on checkpoints a recurring risk. Political tension around the PTI is a secondary factor.

countries.name: India
incidents: 31 Oct — Noney district, Manipur: Police said three Kuki men were killed in an exchange of fire with 'unidentified armed miscreants'. A leading Kuki body blamed Naga separatist outfits, which is unverified.

1 Nov — Kangpokpi district, Manipur: Security forces recovered the bodies of two Kuki men who had gone missing earlier in the week. Large crowds joined protests in Imphal and elsewhere demanding the abrogation of the ceasefire arrangement with Kuki armed groups.

4 Nov — Taodaijang village, Khoupum, Noney, Manipur: A predawn gunfight between rival Naga factions (ZUF-Jenchui and ZUF-Kamson) killed three to four militants. Hours later, gunmen fired on vehicles heading to Ukhrul without causing injuries.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Manipur saw at least eight conflict deaths in five days, on both the Kuki–Naga and intra-Naga axes, with mass Meitei protests against the Kuki ceasefire arrangement. Over the next 90 days, expect more tit-for-tat killings and abductions in Noney, Kangpokpi and Ukhrul, factional Naga clashes, and large Valley protests that could turn violent if New Delhi or Imphal moves on the ceasefire question. Security forces will step up operations against groups outside peace talks. In Jammu and Kashmir, the last infiltration attempts before snow closes the passes (Keran, Krishna Ghati) remain likely, but no J&K fatality was found this week. India–Pakistan tension remains a background factor without direct military incidents.

countries.name: China
incidents: 30 Oct — Scarborough Shoal: The PLA Southern Theater Command said its naval and air forces conducted 'combat-readiness patrols' in the shoal's territorial sea and airspace, calling them a countermeasure to Philippine 'provocations'. The China Coast Guard held 'law-enforcement patrols' the same day.

2–3 Nov — Around Taiwan: The PLA flew 49 aircraft and deployed 6 warships alongside 6 government vessels in the 24 hours to 06:00 on 3 Nov, a sharp rise from single-digit daily counts in late October. INDSR analysts call it an undeclared 'quiet exercise'.

2 Nov — Okinawa–Miyako gap: Japan's Joint Staff reported Chinese WZ-7 high-altitude reconnaissance drones flying between the East China Sea and the Pacific before returning toward the mainland, and Japan scrambled fighters.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. China's own territory faces no armed threat and internal security is stable. Over the next 90 days, expect Beijing to raise pressure in the grey zone and in the air. That includes spikes of unannounced 'quiet exercise' activity around Taiwan, normalised PLA 'combat-readiness patrols' and CCG enforcement at Scarborough, carrier operations east of the Philippines (the Liaoning remains there) with a possible Shandong long-range drill in mid-December, and drone and ISR flights through the Ryukyu gaps. A named large-scale Taiwan drill in the November–December window remains a meaningful possibility. The main risk is a collision or close encounter at sea or in the air.

countries.name: Taiwan
incidents: 2–3 Nov — Around Taiwan: The MND tracked 49 PLA aircraft, 6 PLAN warships and 6 official ships in the 24 hours to 06:00 on 3 Nov, the highest one-day count in weeks. INDSR analyst Su Tzu-yun called it a 'quiet exercise' meant to normalise intrusive operations, and linked it to a US-Japan-ROK statement on cross-Strait stability.

3 Nov — Taiwan: A servicemember was burned in a howitzer fire during readiness exercises, and Taiwanese equities fell more than 3.5% amid the surge in PLA activity. The Mainland Affairs Council warned that Beijing is likely to step up military harassment and interference ahead of Taiwan's local elections.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. The return to a near-50-aircraft day shows that the late-October lull did not mean a lower threat. Over the next 90 days, the November–December peak training window is the most likely time for a named encirclement drill, or for more unannounced surges like that of 2–3 Nov. Triggers could include trilateral statements on Taiwan, US arms decisions or the run-up to local elections. Expect a continuing daily presence of PLAN and official ships, CCG pressure on Pratas and Kinmen, median-line crossings, and cognitive and election-interference operations.

countries.name: Philippines
incidents: 29 Oct — Scarborough (Bajo de Masinloc) Shoal: A PCG maritime domain awareness flight counted three CCG ships, five Chinese maritime militia vessels and a PLAN warship. It also saw a Chinese vessel inside the lagoon towing a smaller boat and carrying an orange, boat-shaped craft fitted with sensors and antennas.

30 Oct — Scarborough Shoal: The PLA Southern Theater Command announced naval and air 'combat-readiness patrols' in the shoal's territorial sea and airspace, and the CCG announced parallel 'law-enforcement patrols'.

3 Nov — Manila: PCG spokesperson Rear Adm. Jay Tarriela said the PCG is still assessing whether the unidentified craft could support underwater operations, and cautioned against calling the ship a research vessel because its markings do not match known Chinese research ships.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Scarborough is becoming a militarised standoff, with PLA combat-readiness patrols, a steady CCG and militia presence, and a possibly underwater-capable Chinese platform inside the lagoon, on top of the October water cannon and collision incidents. Over the next 90 days, expect continued CCG blocking of Philippine fisheries and resupply missions at Scarborough, Second Thomas Shoal and Pag-asa, PLA air intercepts of PCG aircraft, and more PLAN transits east of and through the archipelago, including by the Liaoning. A fatal incident would raise the risk of Mutual Defense Treaty consultations. Mindanao insurgent violence remains low-level, and no significant clash was found this week.

countries.name: South Korea
incidents: 29 Oct — East Sea / Seoul: North Korea fired about a dozen SRBMs from Wonsan, which flew roughly 250 km, a day after Unification Minister Chung Dong-young renewed Seoul's 23 Oct proposal for military talks to verify the MDL and restore communication lines; Pyongyang has not responded.
29 Oct — Paju, Gyeonggi: North Korean propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts were heard from 06:00 for about four to five hours, apparently a test ahead of Kim Yo Jong's threatened border-wide activation.

4 Nov — East Sea: The JCS detected multiple North Korean missiles launched from Sondok, South Hamgyong, which flew under 300 km. Seoul said it is monitoring under the combined defence posture with the US, while the exact missile types are still under analysis.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Over the next 90 days, the DMZ and the East Sea are the twin flashpoints. Frequent SRBM salvos, possible full loudspeaker activation, and continued North Korean MDL crossings met by South Korean warning fire, which Pyongyang treats as grounds for 'self-defence', create a real risk of an armed exchange. The Lee government will likely keep repeating its MDL talks offer while sharing surveillance with the US and Japan. Domestic pressure for a firmer response, including resuming its own loudspeakers, will grow if broadcasts begin. Watch for live fire across the MDL, further mine or drone incidents, and North Korean launches toward the NLL.

countries.name: Vietnam
incidents: 2 Nov — Hanoi: Indian NSA Ajit Doval met Defence Minister Gen. Phan Van Giang to review bilateral defence cooperation. No Vietnam–China maritime incident was found for 29 Oct–5 Nov.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. There were no security incidents this week, but the underlying South China Sea dispute is unchanged. Over the next 90 days, Vietnam is likely to continue hedging through defence diplomacy with India, the US, Japan, Australia and the Philippines, with the Vietnam International Defence Expo on 10–13 Dec as a showcase, while keeping political ties with Beijing intact. It will also keep fortifying its Spratly features. Watch for Chinese pressure on Vietnamese fishermen in the Paracels and Chinese reactions to Vietnamese construction in the Spratlys. A direct naval confrontation remains unlikely.

countries.name: Japan
incidents: 29 Oct — Sea of Japan: North Korea fired about a dozen SRBMs from Wonsan that flew about 250 km, on the final day of Keen Sword. No impact inside Japan's EEZ was reported, and Seoul shared surveillance data with Tokyo and Washington.

2 Nov — Okinawa–Miyako gap: The Joint Staff said Chinese WZ-7 high-altitude reconnaissance drones flew between the East China Sea and the Pacific before turning back toward the mainland, and the ASDF scrambled fighters (single-source report).
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained; watch for an upgrade. Chinese drone and ISR flights and North Korean salvos stayed below the threshold of hostilities, with no airspace violation, EEZ impact or Senkaku incident found this week. Over the next 90 days, expect more WZ-7, Y-9 and intelligence-ship transits of the Ryukyu gaps, possible Chinese–Russian joint bomber patrols, a steady CCG presence around the Senkakus, and Chinese criticism of Type-25 and Yonaguni deployments. More frequent North Korean SRBM salvos raise the risk of an EEZ impact. A close-quarters air or maritime incident, a radar lock-on, or a missile landing in the EEZ would justify an upgrade to HIGH.

countries.name: Indonesia
incidents: 29 Oct — Maybrat, Southwest Papua: Marines detained three alleged TPNPB-OPM members whom the military links to attacks on security posts and on workers on the Trans-Bintuni road project. No new fatal incident in Papua was found for 29 Oct–5 Nov, but reporting from the highlands is sparse.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Reporting from Papua was thin this week, and a news gap is not calm. Human Rights Monitor's Q3 report counts 42 violent incidents in Intan Jaya and 21 in Yahukimo in a single quarter, and late October brought fatal security operations in Nduga. Over the next 90 days, expect continued TNI and police operations (Habema, Damai Cartenz) in Nduga, Intan Jaya, Puncak, Maybrat and Yahukimo, with disputed casualty claims, allegations of unlawful killings and displacement. TPNPB attacks on road workers, drivers, pilots and alleged informants will continue, especially along the Trans-Papua and Trans-Bintuni routes. Jakarta shows no sign of opening dialogue.

countries.name: Thailand
incidents: 29 Oct–5 Nov — Deep South: No lethal insurgent or border incident was found in open reporting; the most recent fatal clash was on 17 Oct in Sri Sakhon, Narathiwat.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. The insurgency has not genuinely diminished: the August coordinated bombings and July's five-ranger ambush show a capacity for bursts of violence. Over the next 90 days, expect intermittent ambushes, IEDs and arson in Narathiwat, Pattani and Yala while Bangkok reshapes the peace process with a new Malaysian facilitator and possibly interlocutors beyond the BRN. The Thai–Cambodian ceasefire is likely to hold despite a residual landmine risk. Stray fire from Myanmar's civil war on the western border is a minor additional risk. A wave of coordinated mass-casualty attacks would warrant reassessment.

countries.name: Bangladesh
incidents: 2 Nov — Mirpur, Dhaka / Gazipur: Thousands of garment workers demanding a 30,000-taka monthly minimum wage, against roughly 13,000 now, blocked highways including the Dhaka–Tangail road. Police fired tear gas and workers set fire to a police vehicle.

3 Nov — Mirpur, Dhaka: Clashes resumed for a fourth day as protesters threw bricks and police fired tear gas and sound grenades, disrupting metro service at Mirpur 11. The Home Minister accused factory owners linked to the former Awami League government of instigating the unrest; a wage board was announced on 1 Nov.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. Unrest is widespread but its lethality is limited, and violence remains criminal, mob, labour and factional rather than organised armed conflict. A rights group counts 187 mob killings and 73 political-clash deaths in the first nine months of 2026. Over the next 90 days, expect continued garment-sector protests and clashes in Dhaka, Gazipur and Savar until the wage board delivers, along with mob killings, gang shootings in Khulna and BNP–Jamaat friction. The government's framing of labour unrest as Awami League sabotage risks harsher crackdowns. An upgrade would be warranted if protests become widely lethal or if the Awami League question triggers street violence.

countries.name: Sri Lanka
incidents: 2 Nov — Kappalthurai, Trincomalee: Gunmen, reportedly armed with a T-56 rifle, fired on a three-wheeler, killing one man and wounding two. Police suspect a drug-trafficking dispute.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. Over the next 90 days, Sri Lanka's security situation will remain dominated by underworld and narcotics-linked shootings, now also in the Eastern Province. These will be met by police and STF operations under the anti-drug drive, with continued scrutiny of police shootouts and custodial deaths. No indicators of insurgent, terrorist or communal conflict were observed.

regions.name: Americas
overview: Haiti has become the region's main military theatre. El Salvador now has about 2,000 troops in the country, more than the whole UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, and most of them operate outside the GSF's command, according to the UN. On 2 November Salvadoran armoured units, backed by Haitian police and the GSF, made their first large ground push into the Plaine du Cul-de-Sac, reportedly killing at least a dozen 400 Mawozo and Chen Mechan fighters. Gang leader Wilson Joseph has asked the UN to mediate, which the UN says is not grounds for formal talks. The four technicians kidnapped on 18 October are still unaccounted for, with no proof of life. Prime Minister Fils-Aime has endorsed a 'common strategy' with the Salvadoran force.

Colombia's armed groups answered the government's bombing campaign with a wave of attacks over the 31 October–1 November weekend. A motorcycle bomb in Algeciras (Huila) killed a police officer. A truck bomb and drones near a military base in Planadas (Tolima) killed four civilians, including a two-month-old baby. Further explosive attacks hit Balboa, La Sierra and Totoro in Cauca. Drone attacks then killed two soldiers in San Jose del Palmar (Choco) and wounded two in El Tarra (Catatumbo). On 2 November President De la Espriella promised to intensify the bombings and resume aerial fumigation. He has ordered six bombing raids in 82 days and is aiming for about twelve in his first 100.

Governments along the Andean–Pacific belt are leaning on emergency powers against organised crime. Ecuador's fourth curfew of 2026 began on 1 November in Guayas, Manabi, Los Rios, El Oro and Esmeraldas and runs to 10 November. Authorities reported 491 arrests in the first two nights, and a two-year-old girl died in Manta after being shot during an extortion kidnapping. Local elections follow on 29 November. In Peru, extortion gangs killed bus and colectivo drivers in Carabayllo (1 Nov) and Chorrillos (3 Nov), even under the extended Lima/Callao state of emergency and ahead of Pope Leo XIV's visit on 11–16 November.

Elsewhere, pressure is political and humanitarian rather than armed. In Venezuela, interim president Delcy Rodriguez unveiled a 'Plan 2040' and promised internationally observed elections, but set no date, while Machado projects a 2027 vote and some political prisoners are being released. Cuba's grid is meeting only about a third of peak demand, with evening shortfalls near 1,900–1,960 MW every day, and short detentions of independent voices continue. The Dominican Republic insists its heavily reinforced border is calm but says it could close it if the Salvadoran offensive pushes gangs east. Bolivia's Morales-aligned sectors have called a national march on La Paz for 6 November, after earlier marches were postponed for lack of turnout.

countries.name: Venezuela
incidents: 2 Nov — Venezuela: Political prisoner Magbis Rondon, held since 2019 after his arrest by FAES and SEBIN agents, was released after seven years in detention (Tal Cual).

3 Nov — Caracas: Interim President Delcy Rodriguez presented a government development plan running to 2040 and promised elections with international observers, but set no date. Machado separately said the transition is heading toward a presidential election in 2027 and denied contacts with the interim government.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. This week brought no clashes, casualties or mass detentions. The political contest after Machado's 25 October return is being fought through statements, an economic plan and selective prisoner releases, which is political tension with limited violence. The Rodriguez government is trying to present itself as indispensable to stability and economic recovery, which IMF figures put against inflation of around 468%, while holding back an election date. Over the next 90 days, expect Machado to build pressure through rallies and demands for an electoral timetable and the release of all political prisoners. The government will likely mix releases with targeted arrests of returning or mobilising opposition figures, as in the September arrest of Javier Oropeza. The Colombian border states remain exposed to ELN and dissident movement as Bogota's bombing campaign intensifies. Upgrade to HIGH if Machado is detained or attacked, if rallies are dispersed with casualties, or if armed spillover from Colombia produces fighting on Venezuelan soil.

countries.name: Colombia
incidents: 31 Oct — Algeciras, Huila: A motorcycle loaded with explosives detonated near a shopping centre during a police inspection, killing Patrolman Julian Esmith Castano Lopez. Explosive attacks and armed harassment were also reported over the same weekend in Balboa, La Sierra and Totoro (Cauca).

1 Nov — Planadas, Tolima: An attack using a truck bomb and explosive drones near a military base and the Aeropuerto neighbourhood killed four people, including a two-month-old baby, and injured at least 15. A curfew was imposed and the health centre was evacuated. The area is a stronghold of FARC dissident factions; no group has been formally identified.
2–3 Nov — San Jose del Palmar, Choco: Repeated drone attacks on troops of Ground Operations Battalion No. 25 killed two soldiers and wounded five. The army attributed the attack to the ELN.

3 Nov — El Tarra, Norte de Santander (Catatumbo): A drone attack wounded two soldiers shortly before a presidential visit. On 2 November President De la Espriella said bombings of 'legitimate military targets' would continue, special operations would intensify and aerial fumigation would resume.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained.
