In a single weekend, coordinated bomb and drone attacks across Huila, Tolima and Cauca killed at least five people, and drone strikes killed or wounded soldiers in Choco and Catatumbo. Armed groups still hold territory in Cauca, Catatumbo and Choco. This is sustained insurgency with regular deaths. The government has made aerial bombing its central tool, with six raids in 82 days, the latest killing six or seven people in Novita (Choco) on 28 October, and it says it will escalate to about twelve in its first 100 days, along with renewed fumigation. Over the next 90 days, expect a cycle of bombing and retaliation: more raids against the ELN, the Mordisco and Calarca dissidents and the Clan del Golfo, answered by drone, car-bomb and harassment attacks on bases, police stations and towns, with a growing risk of civilian deaths, as in Planadas. Legal Medicine already reports eight minors killed in military operations between August and September. Resumed fumigation is likely to bring coca-grower protests and blockades in Cauca, Narino and Catatumbo. Watch for a mass-casualty urban attack, ELN reprisals after its Cauca commanders were killed, and pressure toward the Venezuelan border.

countries.name: Haiti
incidents: 30 Oct — Tabarre, Port-au-Prince: Salvadoran troops began search-and-rescue patrols and set up a base near the US embassy, as El Salvador's deployment reached about 2,000 troops. Bukele said El Salvador covers 90% of the costs and would withdraw immediately if the four kidnapped technicians are returned alive.

1 Nov — Haiti: 400 Mawozo leader Wilson Joseph wrote to UN Secretary-General Guterres asking him to mediate talks with El Salvador. The UN confirmed receipt but said the letter is not grounds for formal dialogue.

2 Nov — Plaine du Cul-de-Sac: Salvadoran armoured units, supported by the Haitian police and the GSF, launched their first large-scale ground operation against the 400 Mawozo and Chen Mechan gangs and reportedly killed at least a dozen gang members. Residents protested against the military presence, and the Viv Ansanm coalition reportedly threatened civilians. The burned armoured vehicle from the 18 October ambush was recovered, but the technicians remain missing.

3 Nov — Croix-des-Bouquets: According to Bukele, Salvadoran helicopters repelled a night-time gang attack on Chadian GSF soldiers. The same day, Prime Minister Fils-Aime publicly backed the intervention and announced a 'common strategy' between the national police, the Haitian armed forces, the GSF and the Salvadoran forces.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Gangs still control most of Port-au-Prince and wide rural areas, are holding foreign military personnel and are fighting ground and helicopter operations in the Plaine du Cul-de-Sac. This is loss of state control over a significant part of the territory, now combined with active combat operations by a foreign national force. The Salvadoran contingent operates largely outside the UN-mandated GSF chain of command, which raises the risk of command friction, abuses and civilian casualties. UNA-Haiti has already alleged deadly airstrikes, which Bukele and the GSF deny. Over the next 90 days, expect continued offensives in Croix-des-Bouquets, Tabarre and the Cul-de-Sac corridor, gang reprisals against communities and possibly hostage leverage, and further feelers for talks from gang leaders under pressure. Gangs may also shift operations toward Kenscoff, the Artibonite or the Dominican border. The fate of the four technicians remains the main trigger: confirmation of their deaths would likely bring a sharp escalation by El Salvador. Watch also for UN Security Council debate on the force's legal status, displacement figures and any spillover toward Jimani.

countries.name: Cuba
incidents: 1–4 Nov — Nationwide: The Electric Union forecast evening-peak shortfalls of 1,920–1,966 MW every day. On 3 November supply was disrupted for all 24 hours, with a peak shortfall of 1,905 MW, and on 4 November seven thermal units were out of service, leaving about 960 MW available against demand of about 2,850 MW.
2 Nov — Havana: Police detained independent communicator Adelth Bonne Gamboa. He was released hours later after questioning and fined under Decree-Law 370, the decree used to sanction online posts.

2–4 Nov — Havana/Matanzas: Cubalex counted 677 political prisoners as of 2 November, later revising the figure to 682 verified cases. The US Embassy visited the family of jailed activists Felix and Sayli Navarro in Perico, Matanzas, and repeated its concern, and Amnesty International called for the release of Roberto Perez Fonseca, held in a punishment cell.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. There is no armed conflict, but basic services are still collapsing, with the grid covering roughly a third of peak demand and outages lasting all day, which fits the HIGH signal of collapsing basic services. Repression stays steady, mostly short detentions, fines under Decree-Law 370 and harsh treatment of prisoners. Over the next 90 days, expect at least one more nationwide grid collapse, which in 2026 has repeatedly set off night-time pot-banging protests and street blockades in Havana, Santiago and provincial towns, answered with targeted arrests rather than lethal force. Migration pressure and US-Cuba friction over political prisoners will persist. Upgrade to CRITICAL only if protests coordinate across several cities, security forces use lethal force, or state control visibly erodes.

countries.name: Ecuador
incidents: 29 Oct — Manta, Manabi: A two-year-old girl died of a gunshot wound sustained during the 26 October armed kidnapping at a local shop, in which the captors demanded up to USD 200,000. The kidnapped woman was freed on 28 October and three suspects were arrested.

1–2 Nov — Guayas, Manabi, Los Rios, El Oro, Esmeraldas: The country's fourth curfew of 2026 (Executive Decree 519, 00:00–05:00, to 10 November) began. Authorities reported 491 arrests in the first two nights and 188 military operations, with firearms, almost 96 kg of drugs and more than 200 vehicles and motorcycles seized.

2 Nov — Cotocollao, Quito: Police investigated the contract-style killing of a woman in northern Quito. Police nonetheless reported only three homicides in Quito over the four-day holiday, compared with five in 2025.
countries.coa: CRITICAL maintained. Contract killings, extortion kidnappings and prison massacres continue in the coastal provinces, and the government still treats the gangs as parties to an 'internal armed conflict' under a state of exception in seven provinces and a curfew in five. This meets the CRITICAL definition of large-scale armed violence with regular deaths. The curfew may briefly lower night-time killings, but earlier curfews in March and September showed violence rebounding once they lapse. Over the next 90 days, expect the curfew and state of exception to be extended or reissued, more military-police operations against Los Lobos, Los Choneros and Los Lagartos in Guayas, Los Rios and El Oro, and continued in-cell killings and riots as prison transfers go on. The 29 November local elections are the main near-term risk: attacks on candidates, local officials and polling logistics are plausible in the coastal provinces. Watch for a post-curfew spike in killings and retaliation against police and prison staff.

countries.name: Peru
incidents: 1 Nov — Carabayllo, Lima: Driver Julio Bermudez Dominguez was shot dead by two men posing as passengers. Police are investigating a possible extortion motive.

3 Nov — Chorrillos, Lima: Josue Antonio Perdomo Estrada (41), a bus driver for the Santo Cristo company who had been in the job a week, was shot up to five times and killed. Police are treating it as a suspected extortion case.

2 Nov — Lima: Preparations for Pope Leo XIV's visit on 11–16 November were reported at 95%, against a backdrop of more than 500 homicides and persistent contract killings. A Cuarto Poder report counts 72 drivers killed in extortion-linked attacks so far in 2026.
countries.coa: HIGH maintained. Extortion networks kept up their weekly killings of transport workers in Lima, with two more drivers shot dead this week, despite the fifth extension of the Lima/Callao state of emergency. This is recurring deadly violence by organised criminal groups, although the state keeps territorial control. Over the next 90 days, expect continued killings of drivers and mototaxi operators, more arrests of extortion cells, and renewed strike threats from transport unions after high-profile killings. Security around the papal visit will saturate central Lima and may displace violence to the outer districts. The government is likely to push tougher measures, including treating extortion gangs as terrorists and further emergency extensions. Upgrade triggers include a mass-casualty extortion bombing, attacks on officials or on the papal programme, or violent clashes during a transport strike.

countries.name: Bolivia
incidents: 29 Oct–5 Nov — Nationwide: No blockades, clashes or casualties were reported. Morales-aligned sectors and their faction of the CSUTCB peasant union called a national march from Patacamaya to La Paz for 6 November, after earlier marches were postponed (13 Oct) and paused (19 Oct) for lack of turnout.
countries.coa: MODERATE maintained. No blockades, clashes or casualties were reported between 29 October and 5 November. This remains political tension with limited violence. The main near-term risk is the national march on La Paz called for 6 November against President Paz's economic measures, the IMF deal and the 'Shield of the Americas' agreement. It could converge with separate COB grievances over food prices. The government has ruled out repealing the diesel decree and says it will not tolerate blockades, and the state of exception (to 17 December) gives it the legal basis for forced clearances, which in the May–June crisis produced casualties quickly. Morales, wanted on a terrorism warrant, has an incentive to escalate, but his camp's capacity to mobilise appears weakened. Over the next 90 days, expect intermittent marches and road-blockade attempts, mostly contained. Return to HIGH if multi-day blockades on the main highways resume, clearances cause deaths, or protests turn into calls for Paz's resignation.

countries.name: Dominican Republic
incidents: 30 Oct — Santo Domingo: The government said it is supporting El Salvador's Haiti deployment with logistics and intelligence and has facilitated Salvadoran transit through Dominican territory.

3 Nov — Haiti border: The army showed reinforced border surveillance with additional soldiers, armoured vehicles and drones. About 11,000 troops are deployed from Montecristi to Pedernales, and President Abinader has said gangs will not be allowed to operate within 20 km of the border.

4 Nov — Dajabon, Elias Pina, Jimani, Pedernales: Defence Minister Carlos Antonio Fernandez toured four crossings and said the border is 'totally calm' and the gangs remain where they were a year ago. Presidency Minister Jose Ignacio Paliza urged caution over the arrival of more than 2,000 Salvadoran troops in Haiti and said the border could be closed if necessary.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. There was no organised armed or political violence on Dominican territory this week. The military build-up is defensive, and officials describe the border as calm and open. Over the next 90 days, the Salvadoran offensive in the Plaine du Cul-de-Sac, about 45 km from Jimani, is the main external risk: it could push gang members or displaced civilians toward the border. Expect further reinforcements, continued mass deportations, work on the border fence, and a possible temporary closure if fighting moves east. The Dominican Republic's growing logistical and intelligence role for El Salvador could make it a target of gang threats or a source of diplomatic friction with Haitian actors. The main risks remain humanitarian and rights criticism over deportations and deaths in custody, not internal instability. Upgrade to MODERATE if gang fighting crosses the border, Dominican forces engage armed groups, or cross-border incidents cause casualties.

countries.name: Jamaica
incidents: 2 Nov — Knockpatrick, Manchester: Police acting on a threat-to-life report stopped a vehicle. Police say its occupant, a murder accused on bail known as 'British', opened fire; he was shot and died in hospital.
2 Nov — Scotts Pass, Clarendon: A 73-year-old man was shot dead and two others were injured in a gun attack at a community shop.

3 Nov — Clayton Heights, Spanish Town, St Catherine: Kevin Maitland ('Nachilous') was fatally shot by police, who say he fired at officers; a gun was recovered and INDECOM is investigating. The same day, the Manchester police divisional head called contract killings a growing concern, with more than three suspected cases this year.
countries.coa: LOW maintained. Violence this week was individual criminal shootings and contested police killings, not organised political or armed-group violence, and national murder figures remain on course for a historic low. The main concern is still the high rate of fatal police shootings, three more in St Catherine and Manchester in about a week, along with emerging contract killings in Manchester. Over the next 90 days, expect continued contested police shootings and INDECOM probes, possible retaliation against police in St Catherine after the Sligoville gun battle, localized roadblock protests after police killings, and the usual rise in criminal violence in December. Watch for planned ambushes on police, sustained unrest in Kingston/St Andrew or St Catherine, or a rise in gang feuds tied to contract killings.
